2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that. opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 as pre-emptors filed a case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Gobindaganj being Miscellaneous Case No. 64 of 1984, alleging, inter alia, that they are co-sharers to the case jote by inheritance while the pre-emptees are strangers thereto. Opposite party No. 4 Naheruddin sold the case land measuring 0.51 decimals to opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 by kabala dated 30-7-76 at a consideration of Taka 5000.00 without serving any notice, upon them as required by law. On obtaining the certified copy of the impugned Kabala the pre-emptors filed the pre-emption case on 15-3-79 after making the statutory deposit. It is to be noted in this connection that the registration of the impugned kabala under section 60 of the Registration Act was completed on 2-12-76. 

 8. PW 1 in his evidence clearly stated that the pre-emptees are co-sharers to the case jote while the pre-ernptees are strangers thereto. There is no evidence on record to hold to the contrary. PW 1 also stated in his evidence that the total area of land under their possession is only 10 big has and, as such, there is no legal bar in the way of getting pre-emption. The evidence of OPW No. 1 regarding the application of the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence as a bar against pre-emption has not been corroborated by OPW Nos.2 and 3, and as such, the uncorroborated and solitary statement of OPW No.1 cannot be considered sufficient to constitute a bar against pre-emption. 

 9. The law on pre-emption is a beneficial legislation for the benefit of the co-sharers and contiguous land holders in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that statutory right cannot be defeated by a casual plea of waiver and acquiescence unless a clear case of estoppel is made out against the pre-emptor by cogent and convincing evidence. Vague and indefinite assertions of waiver and acquiescence on the part of the pre-emptor and even a certain amount of inaction or lack of vigilance and indolence on his part cannot constitute estoppel unless by conduct the pre-emptor is proved to be in loco parent is with the pre-emptee and he has taken an active part in bringing about the disputed transfer. In the instant case, I find that the petitioners have failed to prove their plea of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel by any cogent and reliable evidence and consequently the said unfounded plea falls to the ground. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has failed to point out any legal confirmity in the impugned judgment that calls for interference by this Court exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. For the reasons stated above, I do not find any substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners.
